1: The Way of the Great Learning is to illustrate illustrious virtue, to renovate the people, and to rest in the highest excellence. The point where to rest being known, the object of pursuit is then determined; and that being determined, a calm unperturbedness may be attained to. To that calmness there will succeed a tranquil repose; in that repose there may be careful deliberation; and that deliberation will be followed by the attainment of the desired end.
Things have their root and their completion; affairs have their end and their beginning. He who knows what comes first and what comes last comes near to the Way.

The ancients, wishing to illustrate illustrious virtue throughout the kingdom, first ordered well their states; wishing to order well their states, they first regulated their families; wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons; wishing to cultivate their persons, they first rectified their hearts; wishing to rectify their hearts, they first sought to be sincere in their thoughts; wishing to be sincere in their thoughts, they first extended to the utmost their knowledge; such extension of knowledge lay in the investigation of things.
2: Things being investigated, knowledge became complete; knowledge being complete, their thoughts were sincere; their thoughts being sincere, their hearts were then rectified; their hearts being rectified, their persons were cultivated; their persons being cultivated, their families were regulated; their families being regulated, their states were rightly governed; their states being rightly governed, the whole kingdom was made tranquil and happy.
[Great Learning 6 — The root of the tree]

From the Son of Heaven down to the mass of the people, all must consider the cultivation of the person the root of everything besides. It cannot be, when the root is neglected, that what should spring from it will be well ordered. It never has been the case that what was of great importance has been slightly cared for, and, at the same time, that what was of slight importance has been greatly cared for.
3: In the Announcement to Khang it is said: 'He was able to make his virtue illustrious.' In the Thai Chia it is said: 'He contemplated and studied the illustrious decrees of Heaven.' In the Canon of Yao it is said: 'He was able to make illustrious his lofty virtue.' These passages all show how those sovereigns looked upon virtue as the illustrious mirror in which to see themselves — and the mirror does not flatter, and the looking is the beginning of the ruling.

Ten feet of land are not so rich as ten feet of virtue; one inch of virtue is not so rich as ten inches of the love of the people. The treasury is the last thing a ruler should count; the first is the heart of the people, and the people are the treasury, and a ruler who counts the people counts the treasure, and a ruler who counts the treasure counts nothing.
[Great Learning 10 — The governing of the state]

What is meant by 'In order rightly to govern the state, let there be a regulation of the family' is this: The government of one's state is effected by the love that is in the family, extended. For the family is the school of the state, and the love learned there is the law kept there, and the ruler who has learned it at home needs no army to teach it abroad.
